Area.evidence_source: For example, within the context of unforeseen suicides, participants grappled with accepting the deceased men's agency to self-manage; even though such strategies had failed, there was recognition that men who solicited "outside" help were at risk of being seen as weak. In their tacit fluency with masculine ideals, positioning self-reliance as strength-based and health help-seeking as synonymous with weakness, it was clear that participants understood some of the strategies used and challenges faced by the deceased.There was, however, little interrogation about how these same masculine ideals may have limited men, preventing them from reaching out to more fully connect with one another. Related to this were participants' acceptance of and alignments to emotional privacy or stoicism versus expressivity and relating wholly with other men. Reminders abound here regarding the influence of as well as the tensions in and around dominant ideals of masculinity.However, in contrast to Cook (1988) and Martin and Doka (2000, 2011) who argued against construing such approaches as deficits or maladaptive male coping strategies, we suggest that there are some benefits to loosening the constraints of stoicism among men bereaved by suicide. In essence, without assuming emotional expressivity (Martin & Doka, 2000, 2011) as the gold standard for healthy grieving, facilitating men's talk about suicide can norm such discussions, and provide important permissions for men to speak up and about ordinarily taboo issues in destigmatizing ways.Related to this point, the men's feedback about participating in the current photovoice study was overwhelmingly positive, with many men asserting the therapeutic value of talking about their experiences of losing a male to suicide. Drawing from this methodological lesson, it is important for everyone, including health care professionals, researchers, family, and friends, to recognize that while men bereaved by male suicide may feel compelled to restrain their emotions (for themselves and others), it is critical that we all use our influence to make available, and affirm, diverse avenues for men to grieve.
